passages.t: The land west of the Jordan, divided by lot
passages.happening:
The writer introduces the main business of the second half of the book. “Now these are the portions that the Israelites inherited in the land of Canaan, as distributed by Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the heads of the families of the tribes of Israel” (verse 1).

The shares are assigned by lot to the nine and a half tribes, as the LORD commanded through Moses (verse 2). The other two and a half already have their land east of the river.

He explains the arithmetic. The descendants of Joseph count as two tribes, Manasseh and Ephraim. The Levites receive no region, only towns to live in and pasture for their animals (verses 3-4).

“So the Israelites did as the LORD had commanded Moses, and they divided the land” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Three parties share out the land together: the priest, the leader, and the heads of the families. No one man hands it out as he pleases. Joshua the general has become one member of a council.

The lot was a way of asking God to decide. Its exact form is not described. What mattered was that no human being made the choice. A strong tribe could not claim the best valleys, and a weak one could not be pushed onto the stones. Every share, good or poor, came from God's hand, and no tribe could say another had cheated it.

The count of twelve is kept in a particular way. Jacob had twelve sons. Levi's tribe is set aside for God's service and gets no territory. Joseph's two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, each become a full tribe. So there are still twelve shares of land.

The word ‘inherited’ carries the meaning of the whole section. An inheritance is not earned and not seized. It is received from a father. Israel has fought, and the book has said so at length. But when the land is finally handed out, the book speaks of it as a family receiving what its Father had always meant it to have.
passages.later:
The command came through Moses: “Indeed, the land must be divided by lot; they shall receive their inheritance according to the names of the tribes of their fathers” (Numbers 26:55).

A proverb says what Israel believed about the lot: “The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD” (Proverbs 16:33).

A psalm uses the language of this chapter for a life received from God with thanks: “The lines of my boundary have fallen in pleasant places; surely my inheritance is delightful” (Psalm 16:6).
passages.asks: No tribe chose its own ground. Each received what the lot gave. Ask what in your life you did not choose: where you were born, the family you have, the body you live in, the place you have ended up. Ask whether you have been treating your share as a mistake. Ask what it would mean to receive it from God's hand, and to work it well.

passages.t: Caleb at eighty-five: ‘Give me this hill country’
passages.happening:
Before the lots are cast, an old man steps forward. Caleb son of Jephunneh comes to Joshua at Gilgal with the men of Judah, and he reminds him of a promise. “You know what the LORD said to Moses the man of God at Kadesh-barnea about you and me” (verse 6).

He tells the story. He was forty when Moses sent him to scout the land, and he brought back an honest report. The others who went made the people's hearts melt with fear. ‘I remained loyal to the LORD my God’ (verse 8). Moses swore to him that day that the land he had walked on would be his.

“Now behold, as the LORD promised, He has kept me alive these forty-five years since He spoke this word to Moses, while Israel wandered in the wilderness. So here I am today, eighty-five years old, still as strong today as I was the day Moses sent me out” (verses 10-11).

Then he asks. “Now therefore give me this hill country that the LORD promised me on that day, for you yourself heard then that the Anakim were there, with great and fortified cities. Perhaps with the LORD’s help I will drive them out, as the LORD has spoken” (verse 12).

Joshua gives him Hebron. “Then the land had rest from war” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Caleb and Joshua were the two scouts, out of twelve, who had trusted God when Israel stood at the edge of the land the first time. The other ten said the people there were too strong. Israel believed the ten, and a generation died in the desert. Only these two lived to cross the Jordan. Now one old man stands in front of the other.

Caleb has waited forty-five years. For most of that time he walked in circles in a wilderness because of other people's unbelief. Nothing in his speech is bitter. What he remembers about those years is that God kept him alive.

His numbers also help with the dates. He was forty at Kadesh and is eighty-five now. Since the wandering after Kadesh lasted about thirty-eight years, the wars of the first half of this book took about seven.

The thing he asks for is the surprise. He could have asked for a quiet valley. He asks for the hill country of Hebron, where the Anakim lived. These were the very people whose size had terrified the ten scouts. Caleb asks for the place that had caused the fear. He does not boast. He says ‘Perhaps with the LORD’s help’. It is the humility of a man who knows the outcome is God's to give, and it sits beside complete readiness to go.

The words used of Caleb are that he ‘wholly followed the LORD’. The Hebrew says, word for word, that he filled up after the LORD. The same is said of him in Numbers and in Deuteronomy, almost as his title.

Caleb is called a Kenizzite. That name appears in Genesis among the clans linked with Edom and among the peoples of the land. Many readers conclude that Caleb's family came from outside Israel and had been taken into the tribe of Judah. Others take it simply as a family name within Judah. If the first is right, one of the two most faithful men of his generation was, like Rahab, an outsider brought in.

Hebron was already an old and honored place. Abraham had lived near it and bought the burial cave there, where he, Isaac and Jacob were laid. Later David would first be made king there.
passages.later:
God had said of him forty-five years before, “But because My servant Caleb has a different spirit and has followed Me wholeheartedly, I will bring him into the land he has entered, and his descendants will inherit it” (Numbers 14:24).

The next chapter tells that he did what he hoped: “And Caleb drove out from there the three sons of Anak” (Joshua 15:14).

Hebrews speaks of the many who trusted God and did not live to see what he promised (Hebrews 11:13). Caleb is one of the few in the Bible who did. Paul says where every promise of God comes to rest: “For all the promises of God are ‘Yes’ in Christ” (2 Corinthians 1:20).
passages.asks: Caleb waited forty-five years, most of them lost to other people's failure, and came out without bitterness and still ready. Ask what you have been waiting for, and what the waiting has done to you. Ask whose unbelief or failure has cost you years, and whether you have forgiven it. Then ask what your ‘hill country’ is: the hard thing you would ask for if you trusted God as Caleb did.
